From movement capture to biological insight
Expert guidance on study design, tracking, and kinematic analysis for animal movement research
Explore Services About

Wild Kinematics helps researchers and organizations design movement studies, capture high-quality motion data, and turn it into meaningful biological insights.

We help connect the way movement is measured to the questions researchers want to answer.

In biology, many crucial questions can only be answered using high-resolution motion data: How fast does a predator strike? How does maneuverability change across habitats? How do subtle behavioral displays vary between individuals?

Translating animal motion into precise kinematic data can feel like a steep climb, requiring specialized technical knowledge.

You may find yourself in one of these situations:

Unsure where to start with hardware: Choosing camera placements, frame rates, and calibration methods without wasting grant funding on unnecessary equipment.

Overwhelmed by video and tracking tools: Deciding whether to invest in expensive commercial tracking platforms or learn to use open-source algorithms.

Stuck with raw footage: Sitting on hundreds of gigabytes of video without a clear, automated workflow to extract biologically meaningful variables.

Ready to move your project forward?

Get in Touch Explore Services

How Wild Kinematics can help

  • • Biology always comes first. Bringing together biological research experience, experimental design, quantitative analysis, and scientific interpretation to help you obtain measurements that are appropriate, reliable, and most relevant to your biological question.
  • • No guesswork. Whether you want a guiding partner to train your team and set up a practical pipeline, or a specialist to handle some part of the work for you.
  • • Direct collaboration. Hands-on support so you don't have to figure it out all alone.

You bring the biological question; Wild Kinematics bridges the technical gap.

About Me

Camille Le Roy, PhD

I'm Camille. Research scientist, field biologist, biomechanist — but above all, someone who understands the challenges of an academic career.

With a PhD in Evolutionary Biology from the University of Paris and over seven years of interdisciplinary research spanning ecology and biophysics, my path has taken me from the cloud forests of Peru to labs in France and the Netherlands. Along the way, I came to realize a struggle shared by many researchers: we're good at the doing — the experiments, the models, the fieldwork — but we struggle to hit 'stop' and immerse ourselves in the writing.

I’ve been on that road. I know that turning years of messy data into a compelling story is a long, eventful adventure. Having authored eight first-author papers in top-tier journals (including in Science, Nature Communications, PLOS Biology) and served as a reviewer for a range of multidisciplinary journals, I’ve learned the nuts and bolts of turning raw results into a manuscript that actually get published. There's a specific kind of thrill I get from taking messy, complex data and finding the story hiding inside it. It's one of my favorite parts of the work.

Besides research, you'll find me chasing a similar kind of flow state — on a skateboard, a snowboard, or trying (often failing) to stay upright on a slackline. Traveling is where a lot of this started, and I still find my best thinking happens far from a desk.
